entries.modern_form: PIE *dʰeyǵʰ- 'to knead, form, build (of clay)'; o-grade noun *dʰóyǵʰos 'something kneaded/formed' > 'wall; dough'
entries.note: Pokorny IEW 244 dheiĝh- 'Lehm kneten und damit mauern oder bestreichen (Wand, Mauer; Töpferei); auch vom Teigkneten' is exactly Nourai's gloss; AHD dheigh- 'to form, build' cites 'Pokorny dheiĝh- 244'. Wiktionary (Rix LIV 140-141, Kroonen, de Vaan, Beekes) agrees. Nourai's second spelling 'Dhigha' is his rendering of the zero-grade/extended variant (Pokorny gives dheiĝh-, dhoiĝho-s, dhiĝh-lo-s). Two of his branches are weak: the OP 'daika > dīg' branch is rejected by modern Iranian etymology (see nodes 11-12), and the Sogdian, Persian dež and ferdows nodes are cognates/round-trip loans rather than lineal descendants of the parents drawn.

nodes.derivation: OP didā- f. 'wall, fortress' is genuinely attested: DSf (Darius' Susa foundation charter) line 54 'tyaiy didām apiθa' — 'the men who adorned the wall were Medes and Egyptians' (Kent's Lexicon p. 191, which is Nourai's KNT:191). It is the regular SW-Iranian reflex of PIr *daizah < PIE *dʰóyǵʰos: Proto-Iranian *ǰ (< PIE *ǵʰ) gives Old Persian d where Avestan/Median give z (cf. Av. daēza-), and the reduplicated-looking di-dā- shows the OP treatment (Asatrian 2017, 'SWIran. *didā- fortress, walled residence'). The second word is not an attested OP word but Horn's/Hübschmann's reconstruction of the ancestor of dīvār, i.e. *daiza-vāra- 'wall-enclosure' (HRN:133); the JSON form 'děğa-vâra' with ě and ğ is almost certainly a scan misreading of the book's 'dēza-vâra' or 'daiza-vâra' (Nourai writes ž, not ğ, for the sound elsewhere on this page: dež). Modern reconstruction (Wiktionary, after Asatrian and Rastorgueva-Edelman) is OP didā- + *-wāra-, giving MP dēwār.

nodes.derivation: OP didā- 'wall' + *-wāra- (PIr *wāra- 'cover, enclosure' < PIE *wer- 'cover, guard' — Nourai's cross-reference ☞Wer 3 is right) > Middle Persian dywʾl /dēwār/ 'wall' (MacKenzie 1971) > New Persian dīvār/divār 'wall', with regular MP ē > NP ī and intervocalic w > v. The compound is an old SW-Iranian formation, since it shows the OP -d- reflex, not the Median/Avestan -z-. Borrowed onward into Turkish duvar, Hindi/Urdu dīvār.

nodes.derivation: Sogdian δyz / δyzʾ (Gharib's Sogdian Dictionary; Nourai's SOD:151) 'fortress, castle' is real and is listed by Wiktionary among the reflexes of PIE *dʰóyǵʰos beside Av. daēza-, OP didā- and Persian dez/dež. But it is a North-Eastern Iranian cognate, PIr *daizah with the regular Sogdian outcomes *d- > δ- and *ǰ > z; it does not descend from Old Persian didā- (which has -d-), as the chart's arrow implies. The word is correct, the edge should run from the Proto-Iranian/Avestan-type *daiza- rather than from OP.

ref_check.note: SOD_pages.txt leaf 216 (Gharib p. 151), entry 3825: 'δyz' M — δiza (dyz') < OP didā, f. n., stronghold, fort. BBB f 57; STii 3.27'; entry 3826 'dyz' C = δyz''. Gharib derives Sogdian δyz' 'stronghold, fort' from OP didā — exactly the arrow drawn from node #1.

nodes.derivation: Avestan daēza- 'wall' (Bartholomae AiW; Wiktionary 𐬛𐬀𐬉𐬰𐬀) < PIr *daizah < PIIr *dʰaiȷ́ʰas < PIE *dʰóyǵʰos 'that which is kneaded/moulded' (o-grade of *dʰeyǵʰ-). Exact cognates: Skt. dehī- 'wall, rampart', Gk. teîkhos/toîkhos 'wall', Gmc *daigaz 'dough'. The semantic shift is 'kneaded clay' > 'mud-brick wall'. Pokorny 244 lists it under dhoiĝho-s, so Nourai's POK:244 citation is the standard one.

nodes.derivation: Persian dez/dež 'fort, citadel' continues Middle Persian diz 'fortress' (MacKenzie 1971), itself PIr *daizah < PIE *dʰóyǵʰos — the same word as Av. daēza- and OP didā-. The -z-/-ž- forms are Median/Parthian (North-Western) reflexes of PIr *ǰ, not the Persis form (OP didā- with -d-), so MP diz is an old NW loan into Persian; Wiktionary labels dež 'Iranian (Parthian?)'. dežbān 'castellan', deždār 'fort-keeper' are transparent compounds. Dež-pol/Dezful: Wikipedia and Iranica give the town name as Dež-pul 'fortress-bridge', for the fort guarding Shapur II's Sasanian bridge over the Āb-e Dez; the Arabicised form Dezfūl replaces the un-Arabic ž and p (Nourai's gloss 'strong bridge' is loose — literally 'fort-bridge'). Nourai's arrow from Avestan is the usual shorthand for 'Old Iranian'; the Persian word is a cognate of the Avestan one, not its descendant.

nodes.derivation: Avestan pairi.daēza- 'enclosure walled all round' = pairi 'around' (PIE *péri; Nourai's ☞Per 1 is right) + daēza- 'wall'; attested in the Vidēvdād (3.18 pairi.daēzą pairi.daēzaiiąn 'they shall build an enclosure around'). PIr *pari-daizah; parallel formations Bactrian prdyjg, Khwarezmian prdyz, Sogdian prδyz, Armenian (loan) partēz, Old Persian paradayadām (A2Sd, late spelling for *paridaida-). Meaning shift 'walled enclosure' > 'walled garden, royal park'.

nodes.derivation: pālīz 'orchard, melon/vegetable field' is genuine and belongs here: PIr *paridaizah > Old Median *pariδaiza- / Sogdian prδyz (parδēz 'fruit garden') > Middle Persian *pālēz (with -rδ- > -l-, a NW/Median treatment) > NP pālēz > pālīz, Tajik poliz; Wiktionary calls it a borrowing from Sogdian, older handbooks (Horn, Hübschmann) a Median form — either way not a Persis (OP -d-) form, and a doublet of pardīs and ferdows. jālīz is the doubtful item: Persian dictionaries (Dehkhoda, Moin — Nourai's MON:680) treat it as a variant of pālīz, but English Wiktionary derives it separately from a Middle Iranian *gardīz (i.e. from *gard- 'enclosure', cf. gird), so the j- is not a simple alternation of p-. I found no scholarly citation for either view of jālīz; treat the pālīz link as confirmed and jālīz as uncertain.

nodes.derivation: pardīs 'paradise': Wiktionary derives it from 'some reflex of PIr *paridayjah', via a Middle Persian *pardēz (with -ai- > -ē- > NP -ī- and final -z > -s); it is essentially a bookish/late doublet of pālīz and the same word that Greek borrowed. ferdows 'paradise, heaven' is real but the route is a round trip, not the direct Avestan > Persian line drawn: Old Iranian *paridaiza- > Greek parádeisos / Aramaic-Syriac pardaysā (and Hebrew pardēs) > Arabic firdaws (Qurʾān 18:107, 23:11; Arabic f- for p-; Eilers 1962 explains the -aw- as a back-formation from the plural farādīs, which reflects the Greek/Aramaic form) > Persian ferdows borrowed back from Arabic in the Islamic period. Nourai's BQT:1455 (Borhān-e Qāteʿ) glosses are right; only the arrow is simplified.

ref_check.note: Borhan-e Qate' (Mo'in ed.) vols 3-5 are not online in full text (only vols 1-2 on archive.org).

nodes.derivation: Greek parádeisos 'enclosed park, garden of the Persian nobility' is borrowed from Old Iranian *paridaiza- — specifically the Median form with -z- (Greek -s-), not the Persis form *paridaida- (OP paradayadām, Elamite bar-te-taš); Greek -ei- renders Iranian -ai-/-ē-, -os is the Greek ending. First in Xenophon (5th-4th c. BCE; Anabasis 1.2.7, Oeconomicus 4.13) for the Achaemenid kings' walled hunting parks; the Septuagint (3rd c. BCE) chose it for the Garden of Eden (Gen. 2-3), and Luke 23:43 for the abode of the blessed. Parallel Semitic loans: Akkadian pardēsu, Hebrew pardēs (Neh. 2:8, Eccl. 2:5, Song 4:13), Aramaic pardaysā. AHD's root entry lists 'paradise' under Avestan daēza-, matching Nourai's AHD:950.

ref_check.note: AHD online (archived) s.v. paradise: '[Middle English paradis, from Old French, from Late Latin paradīsus, from Greek paradeisos, garden, enclosed park, paradise, from Avestan pairidaēza-, enclosure, park : pairi-, around; see per1 ... + daēza-, wall; see dheigh- ...]'. Nourai's AHD:950 is the 1976 page of this same entry.

nodes.derivation: Greek parádeisos > Late Latin paradīsus 'park; garden of Eden; abode of the blessed' > Old French paradis (11th c.) > late Old English/Middle English paradis (c. 1200 for the Christian heaven; c. 1300 'place of bliss'). Uncontroversial chain (Etymonline, AHD).

ref_check.note: Nourai cites no reference for this node. The AHD paradise entry checked at node #9 (archived https://ahdictionary.com/word/search.html?q=paradise) gives 'Middle English paradis, from Old French, from Late Latin paradīsus, from Greek paradeisos'.

nodes.derivation: No Old Persian word daika 'clay pot' is attested; 'daika-' is Hübschmann's reconstructed ancestor of Persian dīg (Persische Studien p. 65, Nourai's HUB:65), which he and Klein (KLN:469) linked to *dʰeyǵʰ- 'knead clay' as 'earthenware vessel'. Modern Iranian etymology rejects this: Rastorgueva & Edelman (ESIJa 2003) and Cheung (2007), followed by Wiktionary, derive MP dēg from PIr *dai(a)-ka- 'that which is heated/fires', from *daiH- 'to shine, radiate, light a fire' (PIE *deyh₂-; cf. Skt. dīp- 'blaze'), with possible contamination from *daǰ- 'to burn' — i.e. a 'fire-vessel', not a 'moulded clay vessel'. The *dʰeyǵʰ- derivation survives only as a mentioned alternative. The 'Old Persian' label is also wrong: the form is a reconstruction and, in Persis, PIE *ǵʰ would give -d-, not the -g- of dīg.

ref_check.note: HUB.txt leaf 75 (Hübschmann p. 65), No. 594: 'Wenn dēz, dēza Kochtopf zu got. deigan kneten, aus Thon formen (Wzl. dheigh) gehört, ist es verwandt mit Nr. 563 diz, dēz Burg. Ob auch dēg Kochtopf dazu gehört, ist fraglich, da 1) idg. dhigh durch skr. dēgdhi, digdha- nicht gesichert ist und 2) idg. dhoigho- im Neup. zu *dēy werden müsste. Np. dēg (afgh. LW. dēg Kessel) setzt ap. *daika- voraus. Phl. dēg Kessel (Gl. and Ind. 288) kann eine junge Form sein.' No. 599 (same page): 'Besser *daidavara- (Festungsmauer) als *daigavara- anzusetzen ... Falls dīvār (mit ī) die ursprüngliche Form ist ..., wäre dīvār über *diyvār = *did-vār auf ap. *dida-vara- zurückzuführen. Alles unsicher.' Hübschmann does posit ap. *daika- for np. dēg (Nourai's 'daika'), but he explicitly doubts that dēg belongs to the root dheigh- ('ist fraglich').

KLN_1966.txt leaf 256 (printed pp. 468-469), s.v. 'dixie, dixy' (mess tin): 'Hind. degchī, a small kettle, fr. Pers. degcha, dimin. of deg, pot, which is rel. to Pahlavi dēg, pot, Arm. dez, heap, and to OI. dihmi, I smear, anoint, fr. I.-E. base *dheigh-, *dhoigh-, *dhigh-, to form out of clay, to knead, form. See dough and cp. next word [dizdar, fr. Pers. diz, castle].' Klein derives Pers. deg 'pot' (Pahlavi dēg) from I.-E. *dheigh- 'to form out of clay' — the arrow from the root; he does not give an Old Persian form.

nodes.derivation: The inner-Persian chain is sound: Middle Persian dyk' /dēg/ 'cauldron' (MacKenzie 1971) > New Persian dīg 'cooking pot, cauldron' (MP ē > NP ī); Semnani dik, Pashto dēg and Hindi/Urdu deg are cognates/loans. What is disputed is the root: as under node 11, the preferred modern source is PIr *daiH- 'shine, burn' (*dai(a)-ka-), not *dʰeyǵʰ-, so the edge to this chart's root is rejected. dīzī 'small clay stew-pot (and the dish cooked in it)' is usually attached to dīg in Persian lexica (BQT:912/914, Moin), but Wiktionary gives it no etymology and I found no independent scholarly derivation; its -z- would in any case not be a regular Persian development of -g-.

nodes.derivation: Proto-Germanic *daigaz 'dough, that which is kneaded' < PIE *dʰóyǵʰos (Kroonen 2013: 87), with PIE *dʰ > Gmc d, *ǵʰ > g, *oy > ai (Grimm's law); Gothic daigs, Old Norse deig, Old English dāg, German Teig. Nourai's second form 'dîg' is AHD's 'Germanic *dīg-' (source of lady) — a zero-grade *dʰiǵʰ- variant; the modern reconstruction for 'kneader of bread, dairymaid' is *daigijǭ/*daigjōn- (Old English dǣge, Old Norse deigja 'maid', Swedish deja 'dairymaid'). The gloss 'one who kneads dough, lady of the house' is AHD's, hence the 'AHD' ref.

ref_check.note: AHD_watkins1985.txt line 377 s.v. dheigh-: 'To form, build. 1. Germanic *daigjōn in Old English dǣge, bread kneader: DAIRY. 2. Germanic *-dig- in Old English compound hlǣfdige, mistress of a household (< bread kneader; hlāf, bread, loaf): LADY. 3. Extended o-grade form *dhoigho- in Germanic *daigaz in: a. Old English dāg, dough: DOUGH ... 4. Suffixed zero-grade form *dhigh-ūrā, in Latin figūra, form, shape (< result of kneading): FIGURE ... 5. Nasalized zero-grade form *dhi-n-gh- in Latin fingere, to shape: FEIGN, FICTION, FIGMENT; EFFIGY ... 7. Suffixed o-grade form *dhoigh-o- in Avestan daēza-, wall (originally made of clay or mud bricks): PARADISE. [Pok. dheigh- 244.]' (same list online at ahdictionary.com/word/indoeurop.html#dheigh-). Germanic *daigaz 'dough' and OE dǣge 'bread kneader' (DAIRY), hlǣfdige (LADY) are items 1-3.

nodes.derivation: dough: OE dāg > ME dogh/dow > dough (PGmc *daigaz). lady: OE hlǣfdīġe 'mistress of a household', literally 'loaf-kneader' = hlāf 'bread, loaf' + -dīġe 'kneader' (< *daigijǭ/*dīg-); the medial -f- was lost by the 14th c. (hlǣfdīġe > lavedi > ladi > lady). dairy: ME daierie (c. 1300) = dey/daie 'dairymaid' (OE dǣġe 'kneader of bread, female servant' < *daigijǭ) + the Anglo-Norman suffix -erie; the sense narrowed from 'servant's/housekeeper's room' to 'place where milk, butter and cheese are made' (1670s). All three are AHD/Etymonline standard.

ref_check.note: Nourai cites no reference for this node. Covered by the AHD dheigh- entry checked at node #13: DAIRY, LADY, DOUGH.

nodes.derivation: Latin figūra 'shape, form, figure' is a -ūra derivative of fingō 'to shape, mould (clay), devise, feign' < Proto-Italic *fingō < *θingō, PIE *dʰi-n-ǵʰ- (nasal-infix present of *dʰeyǵʰ-): PIE *dʰ- > Latin f-, *ǵʰ > h > g before n (de Vaan 2008: 221-222). AHD glosses figūra literally as 'result of kneading', which is where Nourai's gloss comes from. (The macron/breve on 'figŭra' in the JSON should be figūra; the -u- is long.)

nodes.derivation: figure: Latin figūra > Old French figure > English figure (c. 1200, first as 'numeral'). fiction: Latin fictiō (gen. fictiōnis) 'a fashioning, feigning', from fictus, past participle of fingō (same root) > Old French ficcion > English fiction (early 15th c.; 'imaginative prose' 1590s). Both are standard AHD/Etymonline derivations from *dheigh-; fiction descends from fingere rather than from figūra itself, as AHD's grouping shows.
